newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic vows victory over hatred in elections.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic vows victory over hatred in elections.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, portraying himself as a peacemaker, predicted on Thursday that his leftist coalition would win Sunday's Yugoslav elections.
"The united forces for peace and development...will celebrate a historical victory over hatred, violence and conservativism," he told 6,000 supporters at the coalition's closing election convention.
"In the new era ahead, may our country be free, successful and peaceful, equal to others and linked to other states and peoples."
His message, displayed on multivision screens in the futuristic glass-domed Sava centre, Belgrade's largest convention hall, was of peace, progress, prosperity, democracy and equality.
There was no mention of the wars and sectarian violence which accompanied the breakup of federal Yugoslavia and which the West once accused Milosevic of stoking.

Milosevic's coalition highlighted the lifting of U.N. sanctions as one of its biggest successes, omitting the fact that they were initially imposed in 1992 to punish him for supporting the Bosnian Serbs.
The coalition parties also stressed Milosevic's new image of peacemaker after he endorsed the 1995 U.S.-brokered Dayton accords that ended the war in Bosnia.

"It will work," Petar Lukovic, an independent Belgrade political analyst, told Reuters. "The voters in Serbia are the best in the world -- they have the shortest memory. They can be convinced of anything."

The coalition, comprising Milosevic's Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS), Yugoslav Left (JUL) headed by his wife Mirjana Markovic and New Democracy (ND), led in popularity polls ahead of the vote in the Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro.

Yugoslav Left held its final election rally on Wednesday amid the trappings of communist iconography. But frequent slogans about equality among peoples regardless of race or religion won thunderous applauses.
The blame for the wars and economic disaster of the past five years was pinned on nationalists and conservatives.
Across Belgrade, opposition leaders told several thousand supporters at an open-air rally that Milosevic was the author of their current economic misery.
They also accused the ruling coalition of corruption and ressurecting World War Two divisions among the Serbs when leftist partisans clashed against royalist chetniks.

"They are asking for hatred, new trenches and new divisions, they want to recreate 1941," said Vuk Draskovic, a leader of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition, a broad spectrum of parties ranging from liberals to right-wing nationalists.
Diplomats said Zajedno's lack of coherent policy had hurt its standing. "The only thing these five parties have in common is their desire to topple Milosevic," one Western diplomat told Reuters.
Zajedno has rallied behind the economic policies of Dragoslav Avramovic, who was ousted as central bank governor earlier this year for seeking a Western-style market economy.
Serbia has been rocked by a wave of strikes over the past few months as the economy worsened and standards of living deteriorated.

Milosevic's second four-year term as Serbian president expires towards the end of 1997 and diplomats believe he will then seek for a transformed post of president of Yugoslavia with sweeping powers -- and a seven-year mandate.
